topic.subject: chemistry
topic.title: Working scientifically, safety and evidence
topic.scopeBasis: TGS 2025-26 Chemistry map: How Science Works; TGS 2026-27 assessment skills
topic.overview: Good chemistry is not just remembering reactions. It means asking a testable question, controlling variables, measuring safely, finding patterns and judging whether the evidence supports the conclusion.
learningGoals: Recall the precise Year 8 scientific vocabulary and symbols.
Apply the idea to an unfamiliar example rather than relying on recognition.
Use the command word, show working where needed and include every mark point.
mustMemoriseRules: A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm; risk combines the chance of harm with its likely severity.
Change only the independent variable, measure the dependent variable and keep relevant control variables constant.
Accuracy concerns closeness to the true value; precision concerns how closely repeated values agree.
Repeatability uses the same person and method; reproducibility uses a different person or method.
Put the independent variable on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis, with quantities and units in headings.
A conclusion must describe the pattern and support it with data; an evaluation identifies limitations and specific improvements.

mustMemoriseVocabulary.meaning: something with the potential to cause harm
the likelihood and possible severity of harm from a hazard
a relevant factor kept constant for a fair comparison
closeness of a measurement to the true value
closeness of repeated measurements to one another
agreement when the same person repeats the same method
agreement when a different person or method repeats the work
a result that does not fit the overall pattern

workedExamples.prompt: A student changes acid concentration and measures reaction time. Identify IV and DV.
workedExamples.answer: IV: acid concentration; DV: reaction time.

workedExamples.prompt: Results are 21.0, 20.9, 21.1 and 27.8 cm3. What should happen before calculating a mean?
workedExamples.answer: Investigate or exclude 27.8 cm3 as an anomaly, then repeat the measurement if possible.

practicals.title: Fair-test planning frame
practicals.aim: Plan a valid comparison for any reaction investigation.
practicals.variables: State IV, DV and at least three relevant controls.
practicals.method: Use a suitable range, standardised apparatus and method; repeat each value; calculate a mean; plot the correct graph.
practicals.expectedResult: A pattern supported by repeated numerical measurements.
practicals.safety: Identify chemical hazards, wear eye protection and use the smallest practical quantities.
practicals.evaluation: Discuss resolution, reaction-time error, anomalies and one change that directly reduces the named limitation.

commonMistakes: Calling the dependent variable the factor that is changed.
Writing 'be more careful' instead of a specific improvement linked to an error source.
Claiming a hypothesis is proved; evidence can support or not support it.
examTips: For 'evaluate', write limitation -> effect on results -> practical improvement.
Quote two values when describing a numerical trend.
Never omit units from table headings or graph axes.
beforeStartingPractice: Read the key rules once, cover them, then retrieve them aloud or in writing.
Use MC first for confidence, but finish with typed, calculation, practical or explanation evidence.
After an error, study the explanation; the same concept returns later in a different format and again after 2 and 7 days.
